statement: The Popol Vuh's earliest surviving written form is Francisco Ximénez's 1701-1703 K'iche'/Spanish copy (held today at the Newberry Library, Chicago) of a now-lost c. 1554-1558 alphabetic K'iche' original — dating derived from internal genealogical evidence naming Pedro de Robles as the reigning "Lord Magistrate" of the Nihaib lineage (Adrián Recinos, Popol Vuh: Las antiguas historias del Quiché, Fondo de Cultura Económica, 1947; Dennis Tedlock, Popol Vuh: The Definitive Edition, Simon & Schuster, rev. ed. 1996, both independently proposing this window). What became of the 1554-1558 original after Ximénez copied it is unknown — presumed returned to its K'iche' owners, never recovered. Independently, the narrative content itself (the Hero Twins cycle, the Maize God's death and resurrection) is attested in Classic-period (250-900 CE) painted ceramic iconography (Michael Coe, "The Hero Twins: Myth and Image," The Maya Vase Book Vol. 1, Kerr Associates, 1989), pushing verified narrative antiquity back roughly a millennium before the earliest surviving manuscript.

does_not_demonstrate: That the Popol Vuh's narrative content originated only in the 1550s alphabetic composition, as opposed to Classic-period iconography independently pushing its verified antiquity back roughly a millennium earlier
